title: Jeremiah 51:15–32
context: The LORD’s word sets the Creator against idols in a hymn (51:15–19) that offers a close parallel to 10:12–16, with small differences in wording that are named here without harmonizing. The LORD then addresses his “battle ax” (51:20–23), promises to repay Babylon for what it did in Zion (51:24), calls Babylon a “destroying mountain” (51:25–26), and summons the nations, including the kings of the Medes, against it (51:27–32).

verses.text: “He has made the earth by his power. He has established the world by his wisdom. By his understanding he has stretched out the heavens.
verses.arminianNotes: “He has made the earth by his power.” Arminian readers note that 51:15–19 offers a close parallel to the hymn of 10:12–16, contrasting the Creator with idols.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the creation hymn of 10:12–16 reused here with small differences in wording. Readers in this tradition see creation as the ground of God’s lordship over Babylon and its idols.

verses.text: When he utters his voice, there is a roar of waters in the heavens, and he causes the vapors to ascend from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and brings the wind out of his treasuries.
verses.arminianNotes: “When he utters his voice, there is a roar of waters in the heavens.” Arminian readers see God’s power over weather and nature, which no idol can match.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s rule over creation. Readers in this tradition note that this verse closely repeats 10:13, and they read the reuse as grounding judgment on Babylon in God’s creative power.

verses.text: “Every man has become stupid and without knowledge. Every goldsmith is disappointed by his image, for his molten images are falsehood, and there is no breath in them.
verses.arminianNotes: “Every man has become stupid and without knowledge.” Arminian readers see the folly of idol makers exposed, as in 10:14, since their images have no breath.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see idols as lifeless and their makers shamed. Readers in this tradition note the close parallel with 10:14 and read it as showing that Babylon’s gods cannot save it.

verses.text: They are vanity, a work of delusion. In the time of their visitation, they will perish.
verses.arminianNotes: “They are vanity, a work of delusion. In the time of their visitation, they will perish.” Arminian readers see the certainty that idols will come to nothing, repeating 10:15.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God bringing every false god to nothing. Readers in this tradition note the near repetition of 10:15, without harmonizing the small differences.

verses.text: The portion of Jacob is not like these, for he formed all things, including the tribe of his inheritance. The LORD of Armies is his name.
verses.arminianNotes: “The portion of Jacob is not like these, for he formed all things.” Arminian readers see Israel’s God as the Maker of all, contrasted with Babylon’s idols.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD as the portion of his people. The line parallels 10:16 with a small difference in wording, and readers in this tradition note it without harmonizing.

verses.text: “You are my battle ax and weapons of war. With you I will break the nations into pieces. With you I will destroy kingdoms.
verses.arminianNotes: “You are my battle ax and weapons of war. With you I will break the nations into pieces.” Arminian readers commonly see the LORD addressing an instrument of judgment, though its identity is debated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD wielding an agent to break nations. Some take the battle ax to be Babylon, others the coming conqueror, or Israel; readers in this tradition hold these options without deciding firmly.

verses.text: With you I will break in pieces the horse and his rider.
verses.arminianNotes: “With you I will break in pieces the horse and his rider.” Arminian readers see the repeated refrain stressing the thoroughness of the judgment carried out through God’s instrument.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the refrain’s cumulative force. Readers in this tradition note that the phrase may recall the song of Exodus 15:1, though that echo is suggested rather than stated.

verses.text: With you I will break in pieces the chariot and him who rides therein. With you I will break in pieces man and woman. With you I will break in pieces the old man and the youth. With you I will break in pieces the young man and the virgin.
verses.arminianNotes: “With you I will break in pieces man and woman.” Arminian readers see the refrain reaching every group in society, read soberly as the language of total war and judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment reaching every age and class. Readers in this tradition do not soften the hard words, but they read them as prophetic poetry rather than as approval of violence for its own sake.

verses.text: With you I will break in pieces the shepherd and his flock. With you I will break in pieces the farmer and his yoke. With you I will break in pieces governors and deputies.
verses.arminianNotes: “With you I will break in pieces the shepherd and his flock.” Arminian readers see the refrain extending to rulers, farmers, governors, and deputies, leaving no part of life untouched.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the refrain’s completeness. Readers in this tradition note that the list moves from war to agriculture to government, showing judgment on a whole social order.

verses.text: “I will give to Babylon and to all the inhabitants of Chaldea all their evil that they have done in Zion in your sight,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will give to Babylon … all their evil that they have done in Zion in your sight,” says the LORD. Arminian readers see Babylon repaid for its actions against Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see recompense for Zion’s suffering. The phrase “in your sight” suggests that God’s people will witness the justice done, and readers in this tradition see vindication as part of the promise.

verses.text: “Behold, I am against you, destroying mountain,” says the LORD, “which destroys all the earth. I will stretch out my hand on you, roll you down from the rocks, and will make you a burned mountain.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I am against you, destroying mountain,” says the LORD. Arminian readers see Babylon pictured as a mountain that destroys the earth and will itself become a burned mountain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image of a destroyer destroyed. Readers in this tradition note the vivid reversal: what crushed others is rolled down and burned under God’s hand.

verses.text: They won’t take a cornerstone from you, nor a stone for foundations; but you will be desolate forever,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “They won’t take a cornerstone from you, nor a stone for foundations.” Arminian readers see total ruin, so that nothing usable remains for rebuilding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the permanence of the desolation. The poem’s language is absolute, and readers in this tradition read it as prophetic judgment imagery rather than as a building forecast.

verses.text: “Set up a standard in the land! Blow the trumpet among the nations! Prepare the nations against her! Call together against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz! Appoint a marshal against her! Cause the horses to come up as the swarming locusts!
verses.arminianNotes: “Call together against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz!” Arminian readers see nations summoned under God’s banner to attack Babylon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD mustering nations. These names are commonly associated with peoples to the north of Babylon, though readers in this tradition hold their precise locations with caution.

verses.text: Prepare against her the nations, the kings of the Medes, its governors, and all its deputies, and all the land of their dominion!
verses.arminianNotes: “Prepare against her the nations, the kings of the Medes.” Arminian readers see the Medes named again among those God summons against Babylon, as in 51:11.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Medes as instruments of judgment. Readers in this tradition note that the oracle names peoples and rulers while keeping the focus on the LORD who summons them.

verses.text: The land trembles and is in pain; for the purposes of the LORD against Babylon stand, to make the land of Babylon a desolation, without inhabitant.
verses.arminianNotes: “The land trembles and is in pain; for the purposes of the LORD against Babylon stand.” Arminian readers see God’s purposes certain to be fulfilled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s purposes standing firm. Readers in this tradition stress that God’s declared purpose against Babylon will not fail, a comfort to those who suffered under it.

verses.text: The mighty men of Babylon have stopped fighting, they remain in their strongholds. Their might has failed. They have become as women. Her dwelling places are set on fire. Her bars are broken.
verses.arminianNotes: “The mighty men of Babylon have stopped fighting, they remain in their strongholds.” Arminian readers see the collapse of Babylon’s courage, as its warriors “have become as women.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the failure of Babylon’s military strength. Readers in this tradition note that the image is a conventional ancient picture of military collapse.

verses.text: One runner will run to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to show the king of Babylon that his city is taken on every quarter.
verses.arminianNotes: “One runner will run to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to show the king of Babylon that his city is taken.” Arminian readers see the news of the fall reaching the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the vivid picture of messengers converging. Readers in this tradition read the scene as poetry announcing the fall, not as a detailed record of how it occurred.

verses.text: So the passages are seized. They have burned the reeds with fire. The men of war are frightened.”
verses.arminianNotes: “So the passages are seized. They have burned the reeds with fire.” Arminian readers see the city’s defenses breached and its warriors frightened.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the defenses failing. Some connect the passages with river crossings, though readers in this tradition hold any specific historical reconstruction with caution.
